explanation: No. If your mom and sister are happily letting people believe they’re very involved while repeatedly choosing not to see your daughter, correcting that with the truth is fair—especially after you’ve already tried addressing it privately. Just keep it factual and avoid turning it into a bigger public scene than necessary.

Yes. Your daughter is an adult, and policing her food on her birthday after choosing a hike she clearly didn’t enjoy was controlling and unnecessarily shaming. One donut was not the real issue; your attitude toward her weight and your wife’s "enabling" is what made this hurtful.

Yes. Telling a child to "shut up" is unnecessarily harsh and rude, especially if you haven't tried a kinder way to set limits or asked her parent to help. It's fine to want a calmer birthday, but address it politely.

Yes. Your friend’s partner trying meth once was not your business to police, and mocking him about his sex life to force a response was cruel and invasive rather than helpful. If you were genuinely concerned, a private, respectful conversation would have been the appropriate approach.

You weren't obligated to invite someone you don't like to your party, but you handled it cruelly and dishonestly. Telling him to "f*ck off," discussing the party around him, and then implying you might add him to the list instead of giving a clear answer was unnecessarily hurtful. A direct but respectful no would have been the non-asshole way to handle it.

A brief glance when someone is suddenly standing directly in front of you does not, by itself, make you an asshole. It would be different if you kept staring or were obviously leering, but based on your description this sounds like a momentary look that was misread.

You’re not wrong for not wanting to spend your free time playing in a way that’s become frustrating and less fun for you. You communicated that the added player changes the balance and pace, and you’re allowed to step back if your friend keeps ignoring that. You would only be in the wrong if you were rude to the new guy instead of simply opting out or setting boundaries.

You publicly shared explicit sexual information about your ex without his consent, which was embarrassing and invasive. The fact that it was a compliment does not make it okay, and dismissing his discomfort as "different for a guy" made it worse. He had every right to be upset.

No, you would not be wrong for sending a polite text asking him to lower repetitive noise that is affecting your sleep. Quietly addressing a reasonable noise issue is normal neighbor behavior, and there’s no evidence he’s dangerous just because his music is unusual. Keep the message friendly and non-accusatory.

You would not be wrong if you told her privately, discreetly, and kindly, because a persistent odor issue is affecting coworkers and she may genuinely not realize it. It would only become inappropriate if you were blunt, public, or judgmental about it.

No—being annoyed at being woken 40 minutes early by a blow dryer is understandable in a shared bedroom/home. As long as you bring it up calmly and work on a compromise rather than blaming her for having a morning routine, you’re not in the wrong.

You said you planned to make hot dogs later, not that you wanted them made for you immediately. Your mom was kind to help, but yelling at you for not eating food she chose to prepare without asking was unfair; at most, this sounds like a simple miscommunication.

You’re not wrong for being upset that your mom appears to be changing the original deal about covering repairs. While raising your voice didn’t help, the core issue is that she promised to handle non-gas car costs and is now reframing a needed repair as a gift. The separation may explain her change in finances, but it doesn’t make your frustration unreasonable.

Yes, mildly. It’s reasonable to feel awkward, but this is the mother of his child and an amicable, friendly relationship is normal and often a good sign; the problem was expecting him to avoid her and then sulking instead of communicating. He should have included you more, but being upset that he let her say hello and chat was not fair.

You would not be wrong to tell your parents, especially since your brother is still a minor and smoking is becoming more frequent. This is a health and safety issue, not just you meddling, and the family history of lung cancer makes it more serious. How you tell them matters, but warning them would be reasonable.

No. You are trying to make sure your very ill father has companionship and help eating when the facility and hospital are not meeting those needs, and that does not make you responsible for the family rupture. Your sister and mother may be overwhelmed, but refusing to communicate and dismissing his care needs is the bigger problem here.

No, your request was reasonable: if your mum already knows she can't take you at your preferred time, it makes sense for her to tell you that upfront instead of asking first. Your comment to your sister was immature, but it doesn't make you the main one in the wrong in this situation.

Yes—regardless of intent, describing your explanations as having to "dumb it down" suggests a condescending attitude toward coworkers and your employer. It was fine to explain the technical limitation, but not to treat someone’s lack of expertise as stupidity. This is more general condescension than specifically "mansplaining," based on what you wrote.

At this point, your mother has already told Cathy, so the critical information was passed on and the decision is now Cathy’s. You were right to push for disclosure, but you are not morally required to force medical care on someone who has already been informed and is refusing to act.

You're not wrong for feeling uncomfortable about a near-stranger being added to a two-week international trip without checking with the whole group first. Wanting a say in a long, close-quarters vacation is reasonable, especially if you're shy and expected a small, familiar group. As long as you express it politely and don't treat the friend badly, you're not the asshole.

No—being frustrated by repeated early noise outside your bedroom is understandable, especially when it disrupts your sleep every day. But your neighbor also isn't clearly behaving unreasonably for making normal morning-kid noise at 7 a.m., so this sounds more like an unfortunate mismatch than anyone being awful. Since you are only asking about your feelings and not planning a confrontation, you're not the asshole.

Yes. Even if other drivers are misusing the middle/left lanes, speeding and routinely overtaking on the right creates unnecessary danger, especially for merging traffic and drivers who do not expect a fast car there. You are prioritizing maintaining your preferred speed over driving predictably and safely.

Yes. You made assumptions about an adult woman's capacity based on disability-related traits, then contacted her parents and effectively outed her dating/sex life without her consent. If you had a real safety concern, the appropriate step was to decline the date and, at most, report concerns to the site's moderators—not her family.

You told your wife you'd be home after the 11am ceremony and then disappeared until midnight on your anniversary with no update. Even if service was bad inside, it was your responsibility to step out, check your phone, or let her know your plans had changed. Her anger is reasonable because you left her worried and derailed family plans.

Yes. Excluding your brother’s spouse to accommodate homophobic relatives is discriminatory and effectively punishes the wrong people for your in-laws’ bigotry. If those relatives might cause problems, they are the ones whose behavior should be addressed or whose invitations should be reconsidered.

A possible coin ingestion in an 18-month-old warrants prompt medical advice because symptoms can be delayed and the danger depends on where the coin is lodged, not just whether he seemed fine. Telling your wife to wait and trying to replace medical evaluation with a homemade metal-detector test put cost and your idea ahead of appropriate care. Even if the detector might sometimes detect metal, it would not reliably show whether the coin was in a dangerous location.

Yes. Your manager handled your birthday request badly, but destroying workplace property and taking your anger out physically was a serious overreaction. You were justified in being upset, but not in breaking equipment and creating more problems for everyone else.

You took something that wasn't yours, after she had already made clear she did not want you to have it, and then went through her belongings and took it again. Her not using the keychain does not make it yours, and cleaning her room or giving her other things does not justify stealing from a 13-year-old. The adults backing you up doesn't change that you were wrong.

You chose to make a sacrifice she didn’t know about, then got angry at her for not valuing or reciprocating it. It’s understandable to feel hurt after the breakup, but using undisclosed effort to make her feel guilty was unfair. Wanting more effort from her is valid; blaming her for a decision you made privately is not.

You reacted to an unexpected physical boundary crossing, and it's reasonable to move someone away when they put their face against your chest without warning. Your brother may not have meant anything bad and was likely just scared, but that doesn't mean you had to be comfortable with it. A calmer explanation afterward would have helped, but pushing him away in the moment does not make you the asshole.

Yes. Missing your 12-year-old’s actual birthday for a leisure trip centered on drinking/clubbing with your adult son tells her she is less important than your entertainment, and birthdays at that age do matter even if you celebrate later. The fact that the trip is not yet paid for makes this a choice, not an unavoidable conflict.

Yes. The restaurant was wrong to cancel late, but your angry, abusive text to employees was disproportionate, and that gave them a fair reason to revoke the courtesy free-pizza offer. Escalating to corporate to get compensated again after that was entitled and unfair.

You’re not wrong for being anxious and not wanting to force a social situation that feels uncomfortable. Meeting your partner’s friends is reasonable eventually, but he should respect your boundaries instead of repeatedly pushing after you’ve hesitated. It would help to be honest with him about the specific reason you’re uncomfortable.

Yes. You let a personal history affect someone’s job prospects and then misled your boss with a damaging half-truth instead of either recusing yourself or honestly saying you had a prior personal connection you couldn’t discuss. Your discomfort is understandable, but sabotaging their interview and lying about the reason was unfair.

You knowingly gave false information to get a lower quote, which wasted the cleaner’s time and changed the scope of the job without honest consent. Even if you only expected him to work the booked hours, springing extra rooms and bathrooms on him after arrival was misleading and unfair. His frustration is reasonable because he accepted the job based on the details you provided.

It's fine to find duplicate posts annoying, but publicly calling people out for crossposting to relevant subreddits is unnecessary. If it bothers you, muting subs or just scrolling past is a better response than policing normal Reddit behavior.

Yes, you would be wrong to bring them while they may still be contagious, even if their fevers are gone and they’re on Tamiflu. Flu can spread for 5–7 days after symptoms start, and your sister already made clear she doesn’t want that risk. Staying home is the considerate choice.

Yes, mildly. Refusing to share Wi‑Fi with trusted guests for their phones for no practical reason comes off as unnecessarily controlling and inhospitable, even if they can technically use cellular data. Your friend handled it badly by making a scene, but your rule is still the odd part.

Yes. You came home exhausted, but your wife is pregnant, has morning sickness, is solo-parenting two kids for weeks at a time, and the house being imperfect does not justify unloading on her or calling her a degrading name. The fact that she won't move does not make her your servant, and stay-at-home parenting is still work.

Mildly yes: repeatedly accepting plans and then canceling is frustrating for your friends, especially when it happens most of the time. That said, the bigger issue is that they mock you and make you feel worse, so the better move is to stop agreeing to plans you likely won’t keep and reconsider whether these are healthy friendships.

Yes. Sally is helping raise your children in the home where they live, and your complaint attacks someone who is providing them care, stability, transport, school involvement, and family support that you currently are not able to provide day-to-day. Setting boundaries is fine, but demanding she stop acting like a caregiving adult while still relying on her help is unreasonable and ungrateful.

Yes. You’re allowed to dislike tattoos and decide whether they’re a dealbreaker for you, but trying to get her to cancel or framing her body choices as betraying the team is controlling. Her getting tattoos she wants does not require your permission.

Yes, if you let your sister secretly shadow the date without Greg knowing, that would be unfair and awkward because he agreed to a one-on-one date, not to being monitored. Taking basic safety steps is totally fine, but be upfront or use less intrusive options like sharing your location and checking in by text.

Yes, confronting her at your SO's work event would be inappropriate and likely create drama for other people rather than accomplish anything. You also don't seem to know her actual responsibility or have verified enough facts to justify a public accusation. If you want to address the issue, do it privately and thoughtfully, or direct your activism at the company through appropriate channels.

Yes. You deliberately tracked him down through other people, cultivated mutual connections under false pretenses, and then lied about how you found him, which crosses into manipulative and stalker-ish behavior even if it led to a good relationship. The fact that no one was physically harmed does not make it respectful or okay.

Yes—reusing the exact same best-man speech, especially in front of many of the same guests, would come off as lazy and as making light of a failed marriage. A brief callback joke is fine, but the couple themselves said they’d prefer something new, so doing the full old speech anyway would be insensitive.

Even though oral HSV-1 is very common and you're careful during active outbreaks, it can still spread through saliva even without a visible sore. If people are sharing drinks with you, especially while explicitly asking about herpes, they deserve enough information to make their own choice. You don't need to announce it constantly, but avoiding disclosure in that context is unfair to them.

No. A 10 PM internet cutoff and wake-up rules for a 15-year-old are normal parental boundaries, especially with school starting soon and sleep schedules needing to reset. It may feel strict, but it is not inherently controlling or abusive for a parent to manage bedtime and morning routines at your age.

No. Your family being on the wrong side of the path was careless, but that does not make it acceptable for a cyclist to hit a child and respond with anger instead of checking if he was okay. Since you did not actually retaliate, your anger alone does not make you the asshole.

Yes. A spoonful of Nutella every few days is not a reasonable basis for yelling, and gestational diabetes is not caused by occasional small treats. More importantly, claiming a right to control her diet because she is carrying 'your child' is disrespectful and policing her body rather than supporting her.

You were transparent, set clear platonic boundaries, and proactively reassured your boyfriend, so wanting to be friends with someone you met is not inherently wrong. His insecurity may explain his reaction, but it does not make your normal social behavior inappropriate. The only small improvement is telling him earlier about new male friends to avoid surprises.

You were responsible for the patient’s safety during an early, high-risk mobility session, so it was reasonable to refuse filming while you needed to stay physically close and attentive. Wanting not to be recorded at work is also a fair boundary. In hindsight there may have been other ways to accommodate them later, but not allowing it in that moment doesn’t make you wrong.

Your concerns about the timeline, finances, and childcare are real, but telling her she probably shouldn't pursue her chosen path comes off as dismissive and unsupportive—especially after she supported you through law school. The better approach is to work through the logistics together rather than steering her toward different careers she didn't choose.

Your hurt and anger are understandable, especially if your brother is being excluded because of his disability. But sending a furious email and threatening to cut contact before calmly asking for an explanation would likely make you the one acting badly. If you address it, do it directly and firmly, not in rage.

You weren't wrong to politely call out someone using a handicap space when there was no visible placard or disability plate. Invisible disabilities exist, but authorized users are still generally expected to display the required permit, so your concern was reasonable. Once he refused, it would be best to leave it and report it rather than escalate personally.

You had a month-to-month arrangement, she originally said she'd be gone by May or June, and you gave her advance notice rather than forcing an immediate move. While you could have communicated earlier and more clearly, it wasn't wrong to set an end date that worked for you as the leaseholder and to require actual rent instead of automatically applying the security deposit.

Yes. She paid for the ride, so she was allowed to say no, and you turned a reasonable boundary into a confrontation by challenging her and then using your toddler to guilt her. Your husband is right that you had no idea why she declined, and your comment was unnecessary and rude.

The mother’s story sounds extremely suspicious, but publicly accusing her onstage with obscene lyrics in front of kids was a reckless way to handle it without first verifying facts or reporting it through safer channels. Even if she was scamming people, your performance mainly created a spectacle and risked harming bystanders more than helping.

Yes, if you go there to sit and do homework for a while without buying anything, you'd be using a business's space as if it were a free study hall. Since you go almost every day, it's reasonable to either buy a small item, go less often, or use a library or other free space instead.

Yes—telling him you "hate" a deeply personal gift he spent a long time making would be unnecessarily hurtful. You can honestly but kindly say it makes you uncomfortable and that you don't want to display a stylized portrait of yourself, without insulting his talent or attacking his work.

A surprise family intervention for someone already struggling with severe anxiety and depression was more likely to feel ambushing than supportive, even if you meant well. Concern was valid, but this should have been handled with her consent, a gentler one-on-one approach, or professional guidance instead of springing all three family members on her at once.

Yes. Since the service and equipment were in your name, returning them was ultimately your responsibility, but taking them without giving your roommate a real chance to arrange alternative internet left her stranded for online classes. Your decision was based mostly on suspicion rather than anything she actually did wrong, and texting only after you removed everything was unfair.

Yes. You're playing favorites based on your personal perception, without fairly evaluating staff who work in different roles, and using access to perks to exclude people on purpose. That creates an unfair workplace and is especially inappropriate since you're related to the owner and in a position of authority.

Yes. It was reasonable to ask for enough space or to move seats yourself, but telling her to bike to lose weight was a personal, insulting attack unrelated to solving the seating issue. Her taking up extra space may have been inconvenient, but your response was needlessly cruel and escalated the situation.

Yes, mildly: if you two are actively prioritizing buying a home, using secretly set-aside money on a luxury trip instead of the shared financial goal would be unfair, especially when he is already contributing the bulk of the down payment. The gift is thoughtful, but major spending should be discussed when you’re making big joint financial plans.

You're not wrong for preferring voice practice or ending a connection that doesn't meet your needs, but you are wrong for treating their boundaries like "bullshit excuses" and speaking disrespectfully when they say they're uncomfortable. People do not owe you calls, and if voice practice is required, you should politely move on instead of acting entitled or contemptuous.

You were trying to relate to a topic she repeatedly raised, not to be cruel or insensitive. Her reaction may be understandable if it hit a deep fear, but mentioning your family experience in that context was not unreasonable. A more tactful phrasing might have helped, but it doesn’t make you the asshole.

You weren't wrong to ask for your change back, especially since tipping for delivery isn't customary in England and you genuinely needed the money. The driver may have assumed it was a tip, but that was a misunderstanding, not you being rude. Ordering only ice cream is unusual, but it's still a service the store offers.

Yes. She is a 4th grader showing anxiety and seeking reassurance in a high-pressure environment, and you responded with sarcasm, labeling, and public-ish callouts instead of age-appropriate support and boundaries. As the adult and teacher, it was your job to set compassionate limits without shaming her.

Yes. She was at work in a medical setting and clearly chose not to acknowledge a past sexual/romantic connection, likely to maintain professionalism and privacy; pushing the issue and insulting her memory was inappropriate. Even if you felt awkward, calling her out put her in an uncomfortable position.

Yes. Once he told you he was engaged and then repeatedly avoided one-on-one plans, you should have respected that boundary instead of continuing to pursue him. Joking that his fiancée "doesn't have to know" made it sound like you were encouraging him to hide inappropriate behavior, so his reaction was reasonable.

Yes, even if it wasn’t meant cruelly, calling a new person 'Miss Piggy' without context was insensitive because it very easily sounds like calling her fat. Intent matters less than impact here, especially since you gave her a nickname based on her relationship instead of asking what she was comfortable with.

You were dismissive and invalidating about your coworker’s identity instead of just asking to understand it. Saying asexual people don’t need to come out and that it’s "too much information" reduces a broader identity to private sexual behavior and ignores the social assumptions and pressure ace people often deal with. Asking questions isn’t the problem; arguing with her about her own experience at work was.

You’re not wrong for ending a living situation that clearly isn’t working, especially after extended problems with cleanliness, pet care, and unreliable rent. Inviting her originally does not obligate you to house her indefinitely, though you should give reasonable notice and handle it compassionately because she relied on your offer. The bigger issue would only be if you sprang it on her without enough time to make other plans.

You offered a casual snack, not table service, and your friend’s request for a plate, knife, and fork for a single pickle was unnecessarily demanding. Refusing that extra hassle didn’t make you a bad host, though your tone was a bit snarky. Overall, your friend escalated a trivial situation.

Yes. Being honest from the start about not wanting to parent does not erase your responsibility for creating a child, and choosing to stay absent while feeling "unbothered" makes you the one in the wrong. Your personal struggles explain how you got here, but they do not excuse abandoning your son.

Yes. Once you told them it had been intended as a gift, offering to sell it to them came across as petty and transactional, especially right after an argument. Your friend has a valid reason to feel insulted; you should have just kept, returned, or sold it elsewhere instead.

You handled it awkwardly, but he put you in an uncomfortable position by showing up nearby and expecting to come over without a clear invitation. Ignoring him for an hour wasn't ideal, yet your safety and comfort matter more than sparing his feelings in that moment. A clearer "no" earlier would have been better, but this doesn't make you the asshole.

Yes. Leaving for a month with no contact during your son's mental health crisis was abandoning your parental responsibility, even if you were overwhelmed and burnt out. You needed to arrange proper support and stay reachable, not disappear entirely.

You shared someone else’s early pregnancy news without permission, and early pregnancy is especially sensitive information to keep private. Your mother’s kind intentions don’t change that the disclosure came from you, and Amy didn’t owe thanks for a gift triggered by a boundary violation. It’s good that you recognize that now and plan to apologize.

Your frustration is understandable, especially with a sick toddler and the apparent bump to your car, but public street parking is not reserved by house and your neighbors are allowed to use it. The passive-aggressive territory marking and resentment over them choosing not to use off-street parking make you the one in the wrong here, though addressing an actual collision or bins blocking access would be reasonable if done calmly.

You agreed to dog-sit and then backed out again, and given the history of doing this once before, it's understandable they see you as unreliable. They were rude in how they responded, but that doesn't change that you should have said no up front instead of agreeing and later reneging. Their dislike of kenneling or past teasing doesn't make your canceled commitment okay.

Yes. You weren’t just refusing to speak Spanish; you insulted your coworkers, told them they don’t belong here, and equated language ability with worth or right to be in the US. That’s xenophobic and hostile, especially since bilingual communication at work can be helpful and respectful.

Offering loose change as a joking 'tip' to a retail cashier likely came across as condescending, especially since retail workers generally are not tipped and may be prohibited from accepting money. Your intent may not have been cruel, but the comment put the cashier in an awkward and potentially insulting position.

Yes. You’re making dismissive assumptions about a disabled coworker, calling needed accommodations “special treatment,” and trying to push him out despite no customer complaints and an established pattern your team already knows how to handle. If there’s a genuine operational issue, raise it neutrally and ask how to support coverage, not suggest transferring or firing him.

You pushed staff to serve you a food item after disclosing an allergy and after being told it may contain nuts, which put the waiter in a liability and safety bind. Even if you personally judged the risk acceptable, the restaurant and server were reasonable to refuse. Asking for the manager to override that was unfair to the waiter.

Yes. Based on your own account, you acted on a suspicion your family did not even share and left an intentionally insulting tip without confirming any actual misconduct. If you felt uncomfortable, a better response would have been to speak to a manager calmly instead of punishing the server over ambiguous behavior.

Yes. Setting a booby-trap gift to physically prank your teens is a disproportionate and potentially unsafe response to snooping, especially when you could address it with normal consequences and boundaries. Wanting to "get a laugh" at their expense makes it more about humiliating them than teaching a lesson.

Yes. Having a preference is fine, but saying Italian pizza "actually sucks" during an argument was needlessly insulting and turned your opinion into a jab at something tied to her culture. It was a low blow because you used it to hurt her, not just to discuss food.

Yes. Using a past crime to threaten your boyfriend into staying in a relationship and parenting role is coercive, and it's especially unfair when you both had agreed beforehand to terminate an accidental pregnancy and he is being clear he does not want this. He still has legal obligations like child support, but you cannot force him to be a partner or father figure by blackmail.

Yes. You knowingly chose to have a secret relationship with a married coworker, and his wife’s illness does not make cheating acceptable. If he wants to leave, he needs to end his marriage honestly first instead of using her condition to justify an affair.
